description: We are a small team of speech scientists and engineers who have spent our careers building voice technology that helps people learn, from interactive reading tutors for children to language-learning apps. Outpost Luna brings that work to the Moon. We believe the next generation of explorers should get to practice the mission out loud, long before they leave Earth.
summary:
Outpost Luna is a free, voice-first desktop app for Mac and Windows that lets anyone practice an Artemis Moon mission out loud. In Flight School, a CAPCOM guide teaches the Moon in short spoken lessons. You guess first, then a 3D Moon, real Artemis II crew audio and NASA and youtube videos show why. 

Eight lessons and a check ride earn patches. Then you run a pretend outpost at the lunar south pole for 10 days. You pick a real site, manage power, air and radiation, send rover ice runs, and shelter the crew through real solar storms. A debrief scores your choices with real NASA numbers. 

Additionally a Moon Library lets you fly to 36 pieces of hardware on the Moon, and explore the moon.

NASA open data drives it all: DONKI storms, JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions, LRO terrain, sunlight and ice maps, and NSSDCA records. Every gauge explains its physics with a NASA source.

Our own custom speech AI built for this challenge runs fully on the computer: no account, no cloud, nothing uploaded. You can play by voice, tap, keyboard, controller or hand gestures, so the mission is open to everyone.
details:
What it does

Outpost Luna is a free, voice-first (including other sensing controls) desktop app for Mac and Windows that lets anyone practice an Artemis Moon mission out loud. In Flight School, a CAPCOM guide teaches the Moon in short spoken lessons. You guess first, then a 3D Moon, real Artemis II crew audio and NASA videos show why.

Eight lessons and a check ride earn patches. In the Mission, you run a pretend outpost at the lunar south pole for 10 days. You pick a real site, balance power, air and radiation, send rover ice runs, shelter the crew through real solar storms, and call Houston when Earth is up. A debrief scores your choices with real NASA numbers.

The Moon Library lets you fly to 36 pieces of hardware left on the Moon, each with its source.

How it works

NASA open data drives everything:

- DONKI space-weather records supply 13 real solar storms from 2017 to 2025.

- JPL Horizons supplies the Sun and Earth positions over each site, which decide power and radio windows.

- LRO LOLA, Diviner and LROC supply the terrain, sunlight, ice, temperature and the 3D Moon.

- NSSDCA supplies the hardware records.

Every gauge has a "Why?" card that explains the physics with its NASA source. Anything invented for the game is labelled "Pretend tech."

Our speech AI runs fully on the computer. A arc-transcriber recognizer hears you, fact-check names, get intent and can also tell whether you were talking to the app. A verification text-based streaming tagger also understands names and intent. A tiny "Director" neural model decides who speaks next and action to take in the application.

There's no cloud model and no account, and nothing is uploaded.

Benefits and impact

Watching Artemis becomes doing it. Learners build intuition for why the south pole matters (sunlight, ice, radiation, communications) by making decisions, not reading. Voice, tap, keyboard, game controller and hand gestures all work for every step. Once set up, it runs offline, so it suits classrooms, libraries and homes with limited internet.

Tools

- JavaScript with Three.js and Vite.

- Electron for the desktop app.

- Python with FastAPI and ONNX Runtime.

- C/C++ for the on-device speech engine.

- MediaPipe for hand gestures.

- NASA open data, preprocessed into the app.

- Ordinary Mac (Apple silicon) and Windows 10/11 laptops; no GPU needed.

- AI coding assistants helped write the code. Our AI use is disclosed on the project site.


Creativity

Your voice is the controller. Lessons come back as mission events, so what you learned about radiation becomes the call to shelter the crew. Real storm dates and real Sun positions shape every run.

Factors we considered

- Scientific accuracy: every fact is checked against NASA sources.

- Honesty: anything invented is clearly labelled.

- Privacy: everything stays on the device, and the camera is opt-in.

- Accessibility: there are many ways to control every step.

- It runs on low-end hardware and works offline.

- NASA is credited clearly, with no NASA branding.
